capital: Ramallah (administrative seat; East Jerusalem claimed as capital)
summary: The State of Palestine lies on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean and comprises the West Bank and the Gaza Strip; it declared statehood in 1988 and is recognized by a majority of United Nations member states, and its conflict with Israel remains unresolved to this day.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam was introduced to Palestine in 634–638 by the Arab armies of the time of the Caliph Umar, and Jerusalem became the third holiest city of Islam because of the legend of the Prophet Muhammad's Night Journey and Ascension, with the Dome of the Rock completed in 691. Over the following centuries the local inhabitants gradually converted to Islam and came to speak Arabic, and Ottoman rule from 1517 to 1917 further consolidated the position of Sunnism. Today the Palestinians of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are almost all Sunni Muslims, with an especially high proportion of Muslims in Gaza.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Palestine is the birthplace of Christianity, and the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem are among the holiest sites in Christianity; the local Christian community can be traced back to the 1st century. But after the 20th century, because of the wars of 1948 and 1967, economic hardship under Israeli occupation and opportunities to emigrate, Christians emigrated in large numbers to the Americas and Europe, and their share has fallen from about one tenth during the British Mandate to about 1% today, concentrated mainly in Bethlehem, Ramallah and East Jerusalem, and mostly Greek Orthodox and Catholic.

ranking.name: Others (Samaritans, etc.)
ranking.description: The Samaritans are descendants of the ancient Israelites who follow Samaritanism, centered on the Pentateuch of Moses with Mount Gerizim as the holy place, and who parted ways with Judaism before the Common Era. In history they once numbered several hundred thousand, but after Byzantine and later persecutions only about a hundred remained by the early 20th century. Today there are more than eight hundred, half of them living on Mount Gerizim near Nablus in the West Bank, where they hold the Passover sacrifice every year on the mountain.

religion.background: Palestine is the shared holy land of Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Christianity was born here in the 1st century, and in the 4th century the Roman Empire made it the state religion. After the Arab Muslim conquest of the 7th century, Islam gradually became the mainstream, and Jerusalem became the third holiest city of Islam. It was under Ottoman rule from 1517 to 1917 and then under the British Mandate. After the founding of Israel in 1948 and the war of 1967, Palestinians were displaced in large numbers, and the share of Christians has continued to fall.

ranking.name: Arabic (Palestinian dialect)
ranking.description: Arabic was introduced to Palestine after the Arab conquest of the 7th century and gradually replaced the Aramaic and Greek that had been in common use, and by the Middle Ages it had become the main language of the area. The Palestinian dialect belongs to Levantine Arabic and is close to the dialects of Syria, Lebanon and Jordan, with urban, rural and Bedouin accents each differing. Under Israeli occupation, many Palestinians have also learned Hebrew in order to work.

ranking.name: Armenian
ranking.description: Armenian is mainly used by the residents of the Armenian Quarter of the Old City of Jerusalem. Armenians have established monasteries in Jerusalem since the 4th century because of pilgrimage, and after the Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire in 1915, large numbers of survivors fled to Jerusalem, enlarging the community. But after the mid-20th century, because of wars and emigration, the number has fallen to a few thousand.

language.history: In ancient times Hebrew and Aramaic were in common use in Palestine, and the everyday language in the time of Jesus was Aramaic; in the Roman and Byzantine periods Greek was the administrative language. After the Arab conquest of the 7th century, Arabic gradually became the main language. During the Ottoman period of 1517–1917 Turkish was the administrative language, and during the British Mandate of 1920–1948 English, Arabic and Hebrew were co-official. Today the Palestinian Authority has Arabic as its official language, and English is an important foreign language in schools.

ranking.name: Musakhan
ranking.description: A thick flatbread baked in a taboon oven is covered with a large quantity of onions sautéed with sumac, allspice and olive oil, then topped with roast chicken, drizzled with olive oil, sprinkled with pine nuts and baked, with a rich, tangy flavor.
ranking.history: Musakhan originated in the rural areas of northern Palestine, especially around Jenin and Tulkarm, and is made to celebrate the olive harvest each autumn, to savor the freshly pressed olive oil. Olive trees have been cultivated in Palestine for thousands of years and are a symbol of the Palestinians' connection to the land. In 2010 chefs in Ramallah made the world's largest musakhan, which was entered in the Guinness World Records, and it is regarded as Palestine's national dish.

ranking.name: Maqluba (upside-down rice)
ranking.description: Fried eggplant, cauliflower or potatoes are layered in a pot with chicken or lamb and rice and cooked; when served, the whole pot is turned upside down onto a large platter and presented intact like a cake.
ranking.history: 'Maqluba' means 'upside down' in Arabic, and the dish is hundreds of years old; similar dishes are recorded in cookbooks from 13th-century Baghdad. In Palestine it is a common dish for Friday family lunches and for entertaining guests, and the moment of flipping the pot is the high point when the whole family gathers. In recent years, communal meals around the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem have also made it a symbol through which Palestinians express their identity.

ranking.name: Kunafa
ranking.description: The outer layer is made of hair-thin noodle strands or coarse semolina, with elastic white Nabulsi cheese sandwiched in the middle, baked in butter until golden, drizzled with syrup and sprinkled with chopped pistachios.
ranking.history: There are several accounts of the origin of kunafa, and it is generally thought to be related to court desserts of the Arab empire period. Nablus in the northern West Bank is acknowledged as the capital of kunafa, where the locally produced Nabulsi white cheese is the key ingredient, and during the Ottoman period the local soap and sweets industries flourished. On Ramadan evenings and during festivals, long queues often form in front of kunafa shops, and in 2009 Nablus made a giant kunafa that set a Guinness World Record.

ranking.name: Hummus
ranking.description: Cooked chickpeas are blended with tahini, lemon juice and garlic into a creamy puree, drizzled with olive oil and eaten by dipping pita bread into it.
ranking.history: Chickpeas were among the first crops to be domesticated in the Fertile Crescent and have been cultivated for thousands of years, but the exact origin of hummus is hard to establish, the earliest similar recipes appearing in 13th-century Egypt. In Palestine, hummus is a basic dish at breakfast and in daily meals, and long-established shops in the Old City of Jerusalem and in Jaffa have been run for generations. There are often disputes among Lebanon, Israel and Palestine over who it 'belongs' to.

ranking.name: Falafel
ranking.description: Soaked raw chickpeas are ground and mixed with coriander, parsley, onion, garlic and cumin, shaped into small balls and deep-fried, crisp outside and green inside, often stuffed into pita bread with tahini.
ranking.history: Falafel is generally thought to have originated in Egypt, where ancient Coptic Christians made fried bean balls from fava beans as a meat substitute during fasting periods, and it later spread to the Levant, where Palestinians began to make it with chickpeas instead. It is the most common street breakfast in Palestine, cheap, and seen everywhere at stalls in Ramallah, Gaza and Jerusalem.
